EUROPEAN UNION AGENCY FOR ASYLUM
Foreword
The adoption of the Pact on Migration
and Asylum in May 2024 marked a
milestone in the evolution of the
Common European Asylum System
(CEAS), while also significantly
impacting the work of the European
Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA). The
Agency has been actively supporting
EU+ countries in updating and
optimising their protection responses
in preparation for the application of the
new legislative instruments as of mid-
2026.
The EUAA plays an important role in delivering the Pact and ensuring its implementation. This
is accomplished through delivering tools and services envisaged by the new legislation,
assisting the Commission in preparatory activities and, following Member States’ requests,
assisting with their national implementation plans. Significant progress has been made both at
EU level and by individual Member States, particularly at a technical level. However, there are
still challenges to be addressed to ensure that the EU's new migration management system is
fully operational in June 2026, including sustained political engagement and ownership at
national level in order to address the identified challenges effectively.
Looking ahead to 2026 and beyond, our primary focus will continue to be on supporting
national authorities to implement the preparations necessary in relation to the Pact, as well as
delivering on the new responsibilities assigned to us by the Pact. The Agency will also
continue to aim for higher levels of convergence in both asylum practices and reception
standards. This effort is crucial for ensuring harmonised treatment of asylum seekers across
the Union, with the Pact giving us an opportunity to progress further.
A key achievement in 2025 was the Agency’s first State of Asylum Conference, which brought
together high-level policymakers, EU institutions, international organisations and experts to
discuss the latest developments and challenges in the area of international protection and
migration in the EU. We plan to organise a second conference in 2026 to further explore and
debate topical aspects of our area of activity.
After becoming a formal qualifications provider in late 2024, the EUAA Academy is now
welcoming national officials from all over the EU+ in its dedicated training centre, where they
receive internationally recognised training in asylum and reception matters. In doing so, they
strengthen their knowledge in the EU’s asylum and reception laws and are better prepared to
identify those in genuine need of international protection, while safeguarding their protection
systems.

Mission statement
Vision
To build a resilient and future-proof Common European Asylum System (CEAS) in line with
European values and international law.
Mission
To promote and help European Union (EU) Member States achieve a harmonised European
approach to international protection through support and use of standards, common tools,
expertise, resources and guidance on asylum and reception.
The European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA)’s values outline the guiding principles that
govern all its activities.

Knowledge and Expertise in the rules and legal obligations which form the CEAS.
know-how

Legal mandate and tasks
In January 2022, Regulation (EU) 2021/2303 of the European Parliament and of the Council on
the European Union Agency for Asylum2 (the EUAA Regulation) entered into force, replacing
Regulation 439/20103 and establishing the EUAA as a fully-fledged agency with a broadened
and enhanced mandate in the area of asylum.
As a centre of expertise on asylum, the EUAA is to contribute to efficient and uniform
application of the Union law on asylum in a manner that fully respects fundamental rights. To
this end it contributes to facilitating the implementation and improving the functioning of the
CEAS.
Objectives of the EUAA4
• strengthen practical cooperation and information exchange among Member States
on asylum-related matters;
• promote Union law and operational standards to ensure a high degree of uniformity
as regards asylum procedures, reception conditions and the assessment of
protection needs across the EU;
• monitor the operational and technical application of Union law and standards as
regards asylum;
• provide operational and technical assistance to Member States, in particular where
their asylum and reception systems are under disproportionate pressure.
To meet the above listed objectives, Articles 1 and 2 of the EUAA Regulation define the
Agency’s mandate and tasks. More specifically, Article 2 stipulates that the Agency should,
inter alia:
• deliver effective operational and technical assistance to Member States, in particular
when their asylum and reception systems are subject to disproportionate pressure.
This should include assistance with the relocation/transfer of applicants for/or
beneficiaries of international protection within the EU, as well as the deployment of
asylum support teams and experts from the asylum reserve pool;
• gather and analyse information on the situation of asylum and CEAS implementation;
• provide information on the situation in relevant third countries, including by setting up
and coordinating European networks on third-country information;
• develop common analysis and guidance notes on the situation in countries of origin
and provide information and analysis on the ‘safe country concepts’;
• develop operational standards, indicators, guidelines and best practices in regard to
the implementation of all instruments of Union law on asylum;

On 23 September 2020, the European Commission (the Commission) introduced the Pact on

asylum and reception practices and a more sustainable and resilient migration and asylum
process in the EU in full respect of fundamental rights.
The entry into force of the legislative instruments of the Pact was June 20247. Entry into
application for all, except the Union Resettlement Framework Regulation, is in mid-2026.

Section I. General context
Each year, the Agency plans with a three-year outlook. The single programming document
(SPD) provides multi-annual programming and annual planning of activities and resources as
outlined in:
• Article 42 of the EUAA Regulation; and
• Article 32 of the Agency’s Financial Regulation8, as amended.
This SPD constitutes the framework financing decision for the implementation of planned
activities financed under operational appropriations in the Agency’s budget in line with Article
72 of the Agency’s Financial Regulation. Implementation of the financing decision for the
multi-annual work programme is subject to the availability of budget appropriations for the
respective financial years after the adoption of the budget or as provided for in the system of
provisional twelfths.
This financing decision sets out the following for the annual work programme:
• for grants: the type of applicants targeted by the call for proposals or direct award and
the global budgetary envelope reserved for the grants (annex XI);
• for procurement: the global budgetary envelope reserved for procurements, the
indicative number and type of contracts, including their subject in generic terms, and
the indicative timeframe for launching the procedures (annex XI c);
• for remunerated external experts: the operational appropriations for their remuneration
under Article 237 of the EU General Financial Regulation9 (annex XI c).
As the EUAA does not award prizes, no details are provided in this SPD.
Policy and geopolitical context
Globally, the asylum policy context is characterised by geopolitical fragmentation10, escalating
conflicts and complex emergencies11, further aggravated by the fact that they often take place
in the regions most affected by climate change. By the end of 2024, 123.2 million people
worldwide were forcibly displaced, marking a 6 % increase compared to the end of 202312.
This rising trend is likely to be exacerbated by a range of issues, including Russia’s continued
war of aggression against Ukraine, a multitude of armed conflicts and various economic
factors as well as water scarcity and food security-related crises13. While asylum seeker flows

cannot currently be predicted with a high degree of accuracy, there is no doubt that triggers
like conflict and climate shocks increase the probability of movements of people away from
the zones of turbulence. While most refugees and displaced people tend to stay as close to
their countries as possible14, some will undoubtedly attempt to reach Europe. The international
humanitarian sector has been affected by the deepest funding cuts in its history, with a high
number of people foreseen not receiving the needed help15. The dramatic reduction to aid
provided will make the world less safe, driving more desperate people to become refugees or
keep moving onwards16.
Policy and strategic framework
Existing conflicts and political instability around the world have continued to impact asylum
applications in the EU which in turn places disproportionate pressure, both on Member States
at external borders and, following secondary movements, on other destination countries.
Concurrently, the EU has continued to struggle with a unified approach to international
protection across Member States. Despite the progress made in the development of the
CEAS, disparities in procedural approaches, recognition rates, protection types and reception
conditions persist among Member States, fuelling secondary movements and challenging the
goal of similar treatment for all applicants.
The Pact, which aims to strike a delicate balance between solidarity and responsibility, seeks
to improve Europe's common response to these disparities, increase preparedness among
Member States to deal with multifaceted situations of pressure and address crises more
efficiently. The legislative instruments of the Pact which entered into force in June 2024 will
come into application in June 202617. Both permanent and operational activities of the
Agency will be substantially affected and work for the EUAA is expected to increase across
the board.
In February 2024, agreement was reached on the revision of the 2021–2027 multi-annual
financial framework. It includes a EUR 190 million increased commitment to the EUAA over the
remainder of this period. This is specifically intended to enable the Agency to support the
implementation of the Pact.
In addition to the Pact, the Agency’s multi-annual strategic objectives and its annual work
programme are aligned with Commission’s 2024-2029 policy priorities18, thereby ensuring a
coherent and effective contribution to the Commission’s objectives in the field of migration
and asylum.
Finally, the SPD is firmly rooted in the ambition of the EUAA strategy for 2024–2029, which
aims to both consolidate the Agency’s activities and enable sustainable expansion along a
well-defined trajectory. It encompasses six long-term strategic goals at the organisational
level, linked to the SPD’s multi-annual and annual objectives.

Values-based work
The objective of the EU’s policy on asylum is to develop and establish a CEAS that is inter alia
consistent with the values and humanitarian tradition of the EU. The Agency's 2024–2028
fundamental rights strategy reaffirms the Agency’s commitments in this respect. The advocate
of the strategy is the Fundamental Rights Officer, who will continue to ensure the Agency’s
compliance with fundamental rights and to promote the respect of fundamental rights by the
Agency. This is particularly relevant as the Agency continues to work on addressing the
unique needs of diverse groups within the asylum-seeking population, including
unaccompanied minors, children and other vulnerable groups.
The EUAA also reaffirms its commitment to gender equality as set out in the EU gender
equality strategy 2020–2025 which emphasises that ‘particular attention needs to be paid to
women and girls in the asylum and migration area’. The Agency further recognises the
importance of incorporating a gender perspective into its activities.
Balancing efficiency with procedural fairness
The EUAA is committed to navigating the Pact's broader implications with a forward-thinking
approach. This includes striking a careful balance between enhancing efficiency in processing
applications and upholding the essential principle of procedural fairness. For example, the
Agency is dedicated to prioritising the review and implementation of safeguards and
measures that protect individuals' rights, ensuring that the acceleration of processes across
Member States does not compromise the fairness and integrity of procedures.
Digital change
The Agency operates in the context of fast-moving technological progress and will continue to
focus on digital innovation. As part of this focus, the Agency is aiming to develop into a digital
administration by leveraging technological advancements and digital solutions to optimise
processes and enhance data management. The goal is to explore applications in areas where
digital technologies, particularly in the domains of large language models and generative
artificial intelligence, can bring benefits and foster synergies and efficiencies.
Mis/disinformation and other hybrid threats
Across the EU, public concerns have continued to grow on the future development of
migration towards Europe19. Sudden or sustained increases in irregular immigration are being
instrumentalised as seen in the false narratives on asylum seekers and migration, particularly
on social media, which are gathering traction with the aim to disrupt and sow divisions in

among others, the rising risk of cyberattacks disrupting elections, the economy and public

In such a context, the need for timely, objective and evidence-based analysis has become
even more critical. The EUAA has a crucial role to play as a hub for asylum knowledge,
enabling informed decisions in a complex asylum landscape. Data show that
mis/disinformation thrives in emergencies, in conflict and crisis contexts, where trusted
information is vital24. The Agency will therefore continue to provide evidence for fact-based
policy making, further enhancing its reputation as a trusted source of information on asylum in
Europe. Furthermore, the Agency will continue working on contingency planning and
readiness to support Member States in emergency contexts, demonstrating a united EU front
when a single Member State is targeted. It will also contribute to positive narratives regarding
asylum and refugees, including through engaging media and exploring other efforts to
counter mis/disinformation.
Planning with foresight
Migration induced by the compounding effects of conflicts and unpredictable climate events
has become one of the world’s defining challenges. The prospects for the upcoming years are
even more daunting. The world has entered a state of increasing volatility in which
geopolitical rivalries intersect with a growing number of violent conflicts, terrorism, food
insecurity, etc25. Among the countries with the highest conflict level, most have been
experiencing either sustained or escalating levels of conflict compared to several years ago26.
Many experts anticipate at least a moderate risk of global catastrophes in the next two years,
while some expect even greater turbulence27.
Close-to-real-time insights into events, patterns and trends in asylum-related migration can
inform Member State responses, while forward-looking, evidence-based analyses can support
the Agency’s strategic planning. Quantitative analysis from applied machine learning
combined with qualitative insights from the field and experts will continue to be used to
generate early warning alerts and forecasts that allow for short- and mid-term planning and
feed into the Commission’s forecasting initiatives.

Advancing elements of sustainability

Internal/external factors
A number of factors have the potential to impact the EUAA’s planning and may limit the ability

significant increase in workload. Permanent and operational support, for instance, are

• adjust its resources and staffing, via its prioritisation mechanism, to ensure it meets its
priority objectives;
• implement streamlined recruitment procedures to swiftly fill positions becoming
vacant;
• engage in discussions with the Commission and the budgetary authority on financial

Asylum trends. Approximately one million asylum applications were lodged in the EU+ in
202433, slightly fewer than in 2023. In early 2025, numbers dropped further. Based on current
trends, a working assumption would be that the number of asylum applications within the EU
might continue at reduced levels compared to the two previous years, unless new conflicts
erupt or existing conflicts exacerbate significantly during the 2026-2028 period. In addition,
the possibility of further instrumentalisation of migrants by neighbouring countries should not
be excluded. As a result, the Agency must also be able to support Member States and third
countries to manage the very high number of pending cases while assuring that new
applications lodged after entry into application of the new Pact can be dealt with within very
short timeframes, which will be very challenging. It may also need to maintain or even boost
its presence in countries under pressure. This involves anticipating likely increases in the
years to come, requiring adjustments and extensions to operational plans beyond their current
scope. The Agency’s response will be to:
• continue to monitor the implementation of its activities, making timely adjustments and
rapid mobilisation of resources as necessary, while investing in agile and innovative
strategies to ensure uninterrupted delivery of support;
• support Member States in their preparedness and ability to cope with situations of
mass influx or unexpected events;
• apply the lessons learned from the complex emergency provoked by Russia’s
unjustified full-scale invasion of Ukraine;
• maintain and consolidate the crisis and first response mechanism to rapidly address
future emergency needs;
• improve and consolidate its internal capacity to make use of complementary
resources, including through grants and contingency funding, where feasible and
necessary, in coordination with the Commission;
• prioritise the preparations for the implementation of the Pact, ensuring that EUAA
networks, activities and products are aligned to effectively support this aim.

Section II. 2026–2028 multi-annual planning
1. Multi-annual work programme
This multi-annual programming document is aligned with the Agency’s multi-annual strategy
and contributes to EU policies. The multi-annual work programme provides an overview of the
Agency’s strategic objectives in its four main activity areas: operational support, training and
professional development, asylum knowledge and horizontal activities. It proposes seven
strategic objectives for the period 2026–2028.
1.1 Operational support
The Agency is mandated to provide operational and technical assistance to Member States in
implementing their obligations under the CEAS, in particular where their asylum and reception
systems are subject to pressure. The EUAA’s operational support contributes to the wider
objectives of EU asylum and reception policy, which include supporting national authorities in
achieving higher levels of convergence in both asylum decision practices and reception
standards, as well as ensuring compliance with fundamental rights obligations, particularly the
principle of non-refoulement. With the adoption of the legislative proposals of the Pact, the
Agency is expected to maintain a substantial operational footprint, with an expanded scope
encompassing additional tasks and activities, within the limit of available resources.
Support to Member States is based on operational plans and specific projects, with
prioritisation derived from needs assessments that consider both increased pressure on
Member States and available resources on the side of the Agency. Prioritisation also takes
into account the need to balance competing requests for support as well as the Agency’s
capacity to deploy its own statutory staff to coordinate, guide, and supervise the work of
experts in the field, while fostering close collaboration with Member States.
Interventions are designed with exit strategies that activate when pressure on a host Member
State decreases, while that Member State, in turn, steps up its capacity, ensuring sustainability
and complementarity. The EUAA will further enhance its operational capabilities, including
through the continual review and update of its operational methodologies, quality tools and
procedures as well as personnel deployment management. Further readjustment of the

1.2 Training and professional development
The Agency is mandated to develop, review, plan and deliver training for its staff, the staff of
relevant national administrations, courts and tribunals and the staff of national authorities
responsible for asylum and reception36. In consultation with national administrations, including
those of Member States under disproportionate pressure, the Agency will continue to assess
training needs, as well as design, develop and implement various training and professional
development activities, with the aim of achieving greater convergence in national asylum and
reception practices.
The EUAA, through its mandate of developing an EAC, has been supporting the development
of knowledge, skills, responsibility and autonomy of officials on the ground. In this context, the
Agency supports the practical implementation of the CEAS, convergence between asylum
systems across the EU and the enhancement of quality standards through training activities
that are of high quality and will lead to accredited learning, in line with Article 8(4) of the EUAA
Regulation. This helps ensure that asylum and reception officials throughout Europe have the
knowledge and skills essential to deliver fast and fair procedures in line with EU standards. In
this respect, the Agency has continued to professionalise the learning available for the
multitude of roles in the field of asylum and reception including a plan to accredit this learning,
inter alia through the development of a fully-fledged master’s degree programme aimed at
managers.
The EUAA’s training will be developed and provided within the framework of:
• permanent support activities and ad hoc training support aimed at responding to the
training and professional development needs of national authorities. Such activities
also allow for enhanced cooperation and exchanges between Member States on
training and professional development;
• operational support to Member States subject to disproportionate pressure on their
asylum and reception systems and with regard to the implementation of their
obligations under the CEAS. In this context, the EUAA delivers fit-for-purpose training
to national authorities as part of the support activities under an operational plan. The
EUAA also trains members of asylum support teams to ensure that they are familiar
with the operational contexts in which they will operate and are equipped with the
skills needed to carry out their tasks;
• support to partner countries outside the EU as part of capacity building under the
EUAA's external cooperation strategy, advancing the CEAS’s external dimension to
achieve a common understanding of EU standards in international protection.

The Agency collects, analyses and disseminates information among key stakeholders to
better understand the situation of asylum in the EU. This information is used to develop a wide
range of analytical products, guidance and tools to support asylum and reception
practitioners, decision-makers and policy experts in their daily work and improve the
convergence of asylum and reception practices. Given the wealth of information and expertise
available, the Agency will strengthen its role as the EU point of reference on asylum

In line with the Pact’s aim to further enhance convergence, the EUAA will continue working
with Member States on common analyses and country guidance notes on specific countries of

essential elements for the implementation of the Pact.

2.4. Strategy for achieving efficiency gains
The Pact adds more tasks for the Agency, substantially impacting its permanent and
operational support activities. Even with an improved division of work among existing
personnel, additional human resources will be necessary to execute these new
responsibilities. In one of its first steps, the Agency adopted a programme management
approach to steer the Pact’s implementation, building on the successful experience of the
EUAA transition programme. This approach ensures that the Pact’s implementation is
managed in an efficient and coordinated way.
More generally, the EUAA's approach for achieving efficiency gains is multifaceted, focusing
on streamlining processes, leveraging technology, and optimising resource allocation. The
Agency will continue to implement improvements to its systems and procedures to further
increase efficiency. Simplifying processes, while ensuring compliance with the applicable rules
and internal controls remains a key objective. In doing so, the Agency will ensure that:
• repetitive and labour-intensive tasks are minimised/automated where possible,
allowing for more time on tasks that have higher added value (e.g., digitalising human
resource processes as much as possible through SYSPER and other digital solutions);
• workflows are streamlined by eliminating unnecessary steps and reducing
administrative burdens, enabling a more efficient and agile operational environment
(e.g., reducing the number of actors and steps in workflows and shifting workflows to
digital tools such as SYSPER, Paperless etc.);
• a risk-based approach continues to be embedded across activities so that efforts are
geared towards tasks that require enhanced control;
• resources in administration are kept to a minimum compared to operations, without
jeopardising the essential deliverables of the Agency;
• there is continual improvement by regularly assessing its systems and procedures to
identify areas for enhancement and implementing necessary changes;
• focus is placed on effective knowledge management practices, ensuring that valuable
institutional knowledge is captured, shared, and utilised to improve efficiency and
decision-making;
• reskilling and upskilling of the workforce is prioritised to adapt to new realities;
• efforts to minimise the environmental impact are prioritised by reducing travel and the
number of physical meetings, and investing in environmentally friendly practices; and
• it uses the opportunity of the review of all practical guides, tools, standards and
indicators to rationalise and merge some of these products where possible.
Technologies such as artificial intelligence are likely to play an increasingly important role in
the EUAA's work, including in collecting and analysing data and supporting research
purposes. The Agency will continue exploring how such technologies can advance its
automation and digitalisation agenda while being mindful of the possible risks and ensuring
the necessary safeguards.

• monitoring achievement of the objectives set out in the environmental policy;
• calculating its greenhouse gas emissions for 2025 using the selected standard
applied to the period 2019–2024;
• implementing agreed initiatives and measures to be delivered in 2026 towards
achievement of set targets by 2030;
• initiating data recording and collection of missing data sets using the approach
established in 2025;
• updating the legal register, if required, ensuring legal compliance and addressing
gaps and corrective measures; and
• initiating measuring, monitoring and reporting on achievement of set targets in line
with the framework established in 2025.

Annex IX: Evaluations
Evaluation approach
Requirements for conducting evaluations are laid down in the EUAA Regulation and in the
Agency’s Financial Regulation, and form part of the internal control framework.
As provided in the Agency’s Financial Regulation (Article 29), any programmes and activities
that entail significant spending shall be subject to ex ante and retrospective evaluations.
Evaluations are prospective and reflective feedback mechanisms that promote:
• transparency and accountability;
• more relevant, efficient and effective implementation;
• change management and institutional knowledge building;
• quality results and processes, good practices and lessons learned; and
• coherence, complementarity and added value.
The dedicated Agency-wide Evaluation Advisory Group, established by the Executive Director
in 2021, promotes harmonisation of evaluations within the Agency and facilitates multi-annual
evaluation planning and reporting, synergies and collaboration.
Evaluations are conducted in line with the Commission’s better regulation guidelines, as
implemented in the Agency’s evaluation framework. The latter establishes the criteria for
identifying interventions eligible for evaluation and lays down the common approach to be
followed, thus assuring unbiased evaluations and the required quality assurance.

Annex X. Strategy for the organisational
management and internal control systems
How internal control systems are organised and designed to deliver set objectives
The Agency’s internal control system is documented in Decision No 160 of the Management
Board of 14 March 2024160. The system is built on multiple blocks of assurance, provided by
different stakeholders.
As the governing and planning body, the Management Board is responsible to ensure that the
Agency performs its duties effectively.
The Executive Director is responsible for the day-to-day administration and for implementing
the decisions of the Management Board and the budget. She also has powers of appointing
authority, conferred on her by Management Board Decision No 98 of 19 January 2022. The
Executive Director is accountable to the Management Board yet independent in the
performance of her tasks.
The Executive Director is supported in her role and responsibilities by the Agency’s managers
and staff, which constitute the first block of assurance. They identify and manage risks and take
corrective actions to address any deficiencies in processes and controls.
Internal control and risk management represent the second building block of assurance. They
ascertain the performance of internal processes and systems and identify recommended
corrective actions to improve governance and internal control systems. Both ex post controls
and evaluation play a key role in this second building block of assurance.

Additional assurance on the efficiency and effectiveness of governance and internal controls
systems is provided by the Commission’s Internal Audit Service. As internal auditor of the
Agency, it conducts regular audits and risk assessments of the EUAA.
The Agency’s strategy for the organisational management and internal control systems covers
four elements:
a) Internal control framework
The Agency’s internal control framework is based on the COSO 2013 Internal Control Integrated
Framework and the internal control laid down by the Commission for its own services.
Various controls, checks and supervisory arrangements are in place to ensure sound financial
management, compliance with the regulatory framework, and to highlight any issues or
deficiencies.
Presence and effectiveness of internal controls are assessed regularly. Each financial year the
management assesses indicators161 against which internal control criteria are monitored. The
results of this monitoring are available on the Agency’s website.
Additional insight on the efficiency and effectiveness of internal controls is provided by general
ex post controls by assessing the effectiveness of each internal control component and principle
and monitoring the implementation of corrective actions. In addition, more specific ad hoc ex
post controls might be implemented by a decision of the Executive Director for high-risk areas
or procedures. For example, specific ex post controls verify financial processes and operations
and are implemented regularly based on a well-established risk-based financial ex post control
strategy.
Evaluations also play an important part in the internal control framework.
Based on insights gathered, recommendations and specific corrective actions are addressed to
senior management for re-assessment and endorsement. Their implementation is documented
and monitored through the central register of deficiencies and corrective action plan, which is
reviewed quarterly and published on the Agency’s website.
b) Risk management
In line with the EUAA risk management manual162, the Executive Director performs an annual risk
assessment exercise to better identify, assess and respond to issues that could affect the
Agency’s activities and the achievement of its objectives. The Agency’s management regularly
monitors the central risk register. Quarterly risk management reviews are provided to senior
management and reported to the Management Board.
The risk management process is further improved by the inclusion of the project risk
management methodology into the overall process based on the COSO risk management
methodology.

The calls for proposals or direct awards scheduled to be launched in 2026 are outlined below. The maximum budget allocated for these grants is

Title: Supporting the mentorship programme in Greece (3)
SPD MAO1
objective
Objective: The objective is to contribute to strengthening the protection and resilience of unaccompanied children (UAC) in Greece by

(CEAS).

The EUAA will fund an expansion of an existing successful Mentorship Programme in Greece through the main following

• Appointment of mentors at local level in selected accommodation facilities for UAC (i.e., shelters, supported

• Facilitation of activities organised by the mentors.
• Provision of training, tools and competencies to the mentors, as necessary for the performance of their role.
• Close coordination with the General Secretariat of Vulnerable Persons and Institutional Protection running the
Mentorship Scheme, and other key stakeholders involved in UAC protection, such as guardianship services,
international organisations and NGOs.
Outputs
The funded activities are expected to create the following outputs:
• Mentorship activities delivered through designated mentors at local level.
• Mentors equipped with tailor-made knowledge, capacity and skills to perform their role.

The funded projects are expected to achieve the following results:
• Expanded Mentorship programme at local level by directly involving UAC actors (international organisations or non-
governmental organisations) in its implementation.
• Enhanced protection and empowerment of UAC, with increased capacity at local level.
• Improved trust-building and communication among UAC, with enhanced access to rights and services through peer
mentorship.
• Facilitate the provision of increased access to tailor-made and child-friendly guidance and support for UAC in
Greece.

Annex XII. Strategy for cooperation with third
countries and/or international organisations
Cooperation with third countries
In March 2023, after broad consultations with stakeholders, the Management Board adopted a
revised external cooperation strategy.
The Strategy builds on the Agency’s significant experience and proven added value as a centre
of expertise on asylum and reception, a forum for coordination and a network of contacts. It
determines the overall direction, objectives, and scope of EUAA actions in the external
dimension along two pillars:
• third-country support, and
• resettlement and humanitarian admission.
The Strategy establishes the following vision for the external cooperation of the Agency:
The EUAA will support the full alignment of candidate and potential
candidate countries with the norms and standards of the Common European
Asylum System and will assist other selected partner third countries in
enhancing their asylum and reception systems.
The EUAA will provide Member States with enhanced support in their
resettlement, humanitarian admission activities, and complementary
pathways for third-country nationals in need of international protection.
The Agency’s actions in the external dimension will be guided by the principles of coherence
with relevant EU policies and partners’ interventions, solidarity with partner third countries and
sustainability of capacity-building activities to develop long-lasting national capacities.
The Strategy identifies the following strategic objectives:
• support EU institutions and EU+ countries in the external dimension of the CEAS, in line
with the ‘Team Europe’ approach;
• strengthen partner third-country legislation and asylum and reception systems;
• offer infrastructure and logistical support to EU+ countries’ resettlement and
humanitarian admission schemes in selected third countries;
• facilitate planning, cooperation, coordination, and implementation of actions in the
areas of resettlement, humanitarian admission community sponsorship and
complementary pathways linked to international protection.
In addition, the Strategy updates the Agency’s legal and policy frameworks of reference;
outlines a renewed prioritisation approach to third-country support; develops new ideas for
resettlement and humanitarian admission; addresses questions related to funding and human
resources; highlights the need to strengthen cooperation and coordination with relevant
stakeholders; and clarifies the way forward for its implementation, monitoring, and revision.

The Agency has successfully implemented new ideas from the Strategy, developing a catalogue of
external action services and granting Western Balkan asylum authorities’ access to several EUAA
expert networks.
Cooperation with EU institutions, bodies and agencies
In planning and implementing its external action, the EUAA will cooperate closely with the
Commission and in particular with DG HOME, in line with the relevant working arrangement in
force. In addition, and in accordance with its working arrangement with the European External
Action Service (EEAS), the Agency will cooperate with third country authorities with the support
of and in coordination with the EEAS and the relevant Union delegations.
The Agency will also work closely with other Justice and Home Affairs agencies to ensure a
coordinated and coherent implementation of the EU’s external relations policy. It will engage
with EU stakeholders to promote its work and address challenges by participating in strategic
and operational fora in Brussels, including the Working Party on External Aspects of Asylum
and Migration, the Operational Coordination Mechanism for the External Dimension of
Migration and EU migration dialogues.
Cooperation with international organisations
The Agency’s mandate also provides for cooperation with international organisations, and in
particular with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR),
which is a non-voting member of the Agency’s Management Board. In this regard, the Agency
cooperates with relevant international organisations both in the context of the external
dimension of the CEAS as well as in the context of the Agency’s work in support to Member
States.
A working arrangement with the UNHCR was updated in 2021, whereas a working arrangement
with the IOM was concluded in 2019. An exchange of letters setting out a cooperation
framework with the International Centre for Migration Policy Development was concluded in
2020, while an updated exchange of letters was signed in 2021 with the IGC –
Intergovernmental Consultations on Migrations, Asylum and Refugees.
Other international organisations with which the Agency will continue to cooperate
closely include the Council of Europe and the General Directors of Immigration Services
Conference.
The Agency will continue cooperating with international organisations having a mandate
relevant to the Agency’s work, including through possible further cooperation arrangements or
the updating of existing ones, where necessary. In accordance with the procedure introduced
by the EUAA Regulation, the Management Board shall decide on such agreements, subject to
the prior approval of the Commission. The Council and the European Parliament will be
informed of such agreements.
